sections.heading: Link to the materiality assessment and the ICAAP risk inventory
sections.text: The 2026 C&E materiality assessment of Sustainability Risk, performed annually and updated on material changes and approved by the Management Board on 15 December 2026, concluded that transition risk is material for credit risk in the mortgage portfolio (labels E–G) and in six corporate sector groups over the medium and long term, and not material for market and liquidity risk given the Bank's limited trading book and the composition of its liquidity buffer. The assessment covered transition and physical risk drivers and their impact on credit, market, operational, liquidity, reputational and business model risk, and combined exposure-based methods (sector and label concentrations), portfolio-based methods (alignment metrics) and scenario-based methods (the 2025 interim climate stress test). Materiality thresholds were 5% of CET1 capital for cumulative losses over the medium term and 1% of total exposure for concentrations; each non-materiality conclusion is documented with the evidence and threshold applied. The outcome feeds the ICAAP risk inventory, in which climate transition risk was recorded as a driver of credit risk in the annual risk identification exercise of March 2027, the stress testing programme and the model development plan, which triggered the development of CTR. The measurement approach is commensurate with the materiality outcome: material portfolios are modelled at exposure level, while non-material portfolios (SME retail and consumer lending) are covered by sector proxies in the materiality assessment only, and CTR outputs in turn feed the next materiality assessment. A gap analysis of the Bank's stress testing models by Enterprise Stress Testing (October 2026) found that the credit satellites of MDL-10 contain no environment-sensitive variables; CTR addresses this structurally rather than through ad hoc adjustments, starting with credit risk, and the extension to the banking book bond portfolio and to operational risk is planned for 2028–2029.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: CTR consists of a scenario layer and two portfolio modules, linked to the Bank's existing credit risk parameter models. The scenario layer translates NGFS Phase V long-term and NGFS short-term scenario variables (carbon prices, energy prices, sectoral gross value added and household energy expenditure) for the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany into the model's risk drivers, consistently with the macroeconomic paths of MDL-10. The mortgage module projects label-differentiated house prices and energy-cost affordability shocks per loan and converts them into PD multipliers (via the energy-cost-to-income ratio) and stressed LGD (via indexed LTV). The corporate module projects carbon costs, pass-through, demand effects and transition capex at obligor level for the 250 largest obligors in transition-sensitive sectors (bottom-up) and at sector level for the remaining obligors, which are grouped by transition-risk sector and country, and converts the projections into rating migrations and point-in-time PDs. Both modules produce stressed PD, LGD and EAD per exposure and year, which the stress testing platform aggregates into incremental credit losses, risk-weighted assets and CET1 impact. Segmentation is by label class (eight classes) and dwelling type for mortgages and by 22 transition-risk sectors and three countries for corporates.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: CTR depends on the following approved models: MDL-10 Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (macro paths and macro-driven PD and LGD satellites), the production versions of MDL-01 (PD residential mortgages) and MDL-02 (LGD residential mortgages) for loan-level starting parameters, MDL-06 PD Corporates (financial scorecard and master scale used for rating migration), and the production versions of MDL-07 and MDL-08 (IFRS 9 point-in-time PD term structures). The risk parameters to which CTR applies its climate multipliers are thus produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001. CTR adds only the climate-differentiated component on top of these models: the same satellite model (MDL-10) is used for the macro-driven PD component in stress testing, IFRS 9 and ICAAP, and CTR does not re-estimate macro sensitivities, so that the climate increment is not double counted. The purpose-driven difference is that CTR applies its multipliers to point-in-time PDs for credit losses and to the IRB PD after rating migration for risk-weighted assets (section 5.3). Changes to an upstream model are notified to the CTR model owner through the dependency register of the inventory and trigger an impact assessment under MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Scenario set and narratives
sections.text: The scenario set combines a short-term ICAAP scenario and three long-term scenarios, all based on recognised reference pathways, and is used to test the Bank's resilience to climate risk under different scenarios. Short term (2027–2029): the ICAAP climate adverse scenario CTR-ST-ADV overlays the NGFS short-term 'Sudden Wake-Up Call' narrative, in which an abrupt tightening of climate policy triggers a sharp repricing of carbon-intensive activities, on the Bank's ICAAP 2027 adverse macroeconomic scenario; the EU carbon price rises from EUR 78 per tonne CO2e (2026 average) to EUR 190 in 2028 and EUR 240 in 2029, and household gas tariffs increase by 45% in 2028. The ICAAP baseline embeds the NGFS Current Policies trajectory, consistent with the Bank's reference scenario (common narrative of the most likely evolution of the business environment), which the Management Board endorsed on 10 December 2026 and which is used across business planning and the ICAAP. Long term (2027–2050): NGFS Phase V Net Zero 2050 (orderly transition), Delayed Transition (disorderly transition) and Current Policies (hot house world), with EU carbon prices of EUR 185, 85 and 90 per tonne in 2030 and EUR 350, 480 and 95 in 2040 respectively (EUR 2024 prices). sections.heading: Scenario severity and consistency
sections.text: The severity of CTR-ST-ADV was calibrated against historical and hypothetical events: the 2028 household energy cost shock corresponds to 70% of the peak increase of Dutch household gas tariffs in 2022, and the two-year carbon price increase corresponds to the 97.5th percentile of two-year changes across the NGFS Phase V scenario ensemble and exceeds the largest two-year increase observed in the EU ETS (2021–2022). Consistency between variables is ensured by taking energy prices, GDP and sectoral gross value added from the same NGFS model run, and by applying the ICAAP adverse macroeconomic paths of MDL-10 unchanged. Expert adjustments to scenario paths are limited to the disaggregation of EU energy prices to the three countries (EJ-CTR-08), which is documented and approved under MRM-STD-023. The ICAAP adverse scenario covers GDP, unemployment, residential and commercial real estate prices, the interest rate term structure, credit spreads, equity prices, exchange rates and inflation; CTR adds carbon prices, household and industrial energy prices and sectoral output to this set. The combined scenario is severe but plausible: it reflects the Bank's material vulnerabilities identified in the risk identification process (concentrations in Dutch residential real estate and in energy-intensive sectors) and reduces the CET1 ratio at the trough by a further 78 bp in addition to the ICAAP adverse scenario, consistent with its purpose of testing capital adequacy.

sections.heading: Transmission channels and mitigating factors
sections.text: The transmission channels were identified in a structured process with Sustainability Risk, Credit Risk Management and Economic Research (workshops of 3 and 17 November 2026), building on the 2026 materiality assessment, and are reviewed annually together with the materiality assessment. Mortgages: (M1) energy-label-driven changes in collateral values through the capitalisation of higher energy and renovation costs; (M2) energy-cost-driven deterioration of borrower affordability; (M3) renovation financing needs increasing indebtedness, which is assessed qualitatively. Corporates: (C1) carbon-price-driven costs reducing profitability, net of pass-through to customers; (C2) demand shifts in sectors facing substitution, such as fossil fuels and internal combustion vehicles; (C3) transition capital expenditure increasing leverage; (C4) stranded-asset risk reducing collateral recoveries in fossil fuel sectors. Physical risk channels (flood and subsidence damage to collateral) are covered by the physical risk assessment of Sustainability Risk and not by CTR; within CTR the channels are mapped to credit risk (default probabilities and collateral values) only. Mitigating and amplifying factors are included where material within the horizon: announced corporate transition plans reduce the carbon cost only where capex is committed and financed (credited for 41 of the 250 bottom-up obligors); national subsidies for home insulation reduce renovation costs by 20% in the orderly scenario only; and no additional government support is assumed in the disorderly scenarios.

sections.heading: Time horizons and capital perspectives
sections.text: CTR produces results for three horizons consistent with CER-POL-001 §5.3: short term (2027–2029, the three-year ICAAP normative horizon), medium term (to 2035) and long term (to 2050, in five-year steps). In the normative perspective, the stressed PD, LGD and RWA feed the three-year projection of own funds and capital ratios under the ICAAP baseline and adverse scenarios, which are updated with every ICAAP cycle. In the economic perspective, CTR provides a point-in-time add-on at the reference date, defined as the difference between the credit risk economic capital computed with climate-adjusted point-in-time PDs and LGDs (Delayed Transition calibration of the first projection year) and the unadjusted economic capital, complemented by a medium-term view of the add-on to 2035. The long-term results support the resilience analysis of the business model required by EBA/GL/2025/04, projecting expected loss and the risk-adjusted margin of the in-scope portfolios over more than ten years, and are not translated into capital figures. Climate risk is treated as a driver of credit risk; no diversification benefit between climate and other credit risk drivers is assumed, and gross figures are reported.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: Model development uses the frozen RDS RDS-CTR-2026Q4 v1.0, approved on 12 March 2027 (EVD-19-RDS), whose construction, representativeness and data quality are documented there. Samples were defined before estimation: for the affordability model, the development sample covers 2015–2022 (random 70% of loans), the out-of-sample test the remaining 30% of loans and the out-of-time sample 2023–2024; for the hedonic model, development covers 2019–2023 and out-of-time 2024–2025; for the corporate migration mapping, development covers 2014–2021 and out-of-time 2022–2025. Out-of-time samples were not used for variable selection or parameter estimation. Candidate variables were assessed for economic rationale, availability in the production data of the stress testing platform and stability over the observation period; the label method (EL_METHOD) and label source (registered or estimated) are retained as control variables. The data limitations (estimated labels, proxied emissions) are carried into the limitations log (section 8.2) and into the conservative adjustments (chapter 6).

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Three methodological alternatives were assessed against documented criteria: regulatory expectations, data availability, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation in the stress testing platform. (A) Top-down sector multipliers: PD multipliers per sector derived from NGFS sectoral gross value added through the MDL-10 corporate satellite; simple and transparent, but insensitive to obligor-level emissions and pass-through. (B) Bottom-up financial projection with rating migration for large obligors and label-level mortgage shocks, combined with sector multipliers for the remaining obligors; sensitive to exposure-level emissions and labels and interpretable, but data intensive. (C) Structural climate-adjusted Merton model with asset value shocks from discounted carbon costs; theoretically coherent, but dependent on equity data that are unavailable for 83% of obligors and difficult to reconcile with the Bank's rating scale. Alternative B was selected because it applies shocks at exposure level where data permit, reflects obligor emissions and energy labels, reuses the approved rating scorecard and master scale, and passed the back-tests in section 7.1; alternative A is retained as challenger model (section 7.3). The selected approach relies on transparent regression and scorecard mechanics, so no transparency is traded for performance, and it is tailored to the Bank's business model and portfolios rather than imported from an external methodology.

sections.heading: Mortgage module – energy label house price differentials
sections.text: The collateral channel is based on a hedonic regression of the logarithm of transaction prices on energy label dummies (reference class B), dwelling characteristics (floor area, type, construction period and plot size), municipality-by-quarter fixed effects and the label method, estimated per year on the hedonic sample. The estimated price differential of label G relative to label B widened from −3.1% in 2019 to −7.8% in 2024, with a marked increase after the 2022 energy price shock, which supports the capitalisation of energy costs into prices. Under a scenario, the additional label differential is projected as the present value of the scenario increase in annual energy costs and of the renovation cost to reach label B, multiplied by the estimated capitalisation rate of 0.46, the share of that present value reflected in prices according to the 2021–2024 change in differentials. The resulting peak house price haircuts relative to label C, applied on top of the MDL-10 house price index path, are: label A and better +1.0%, B 0.0%, D −3.5%, E −6.0%, F −9.0% and G −12.5% under Delayed Transition (peak in 2035), and 60% of these values under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario by 2029. Label C is the reference class because its price path is closest to the national house price index; the exposure-weighted portfolio haircut is −2.0%. Stressed indexed collateral values therefore reflect the energy label of each property, as required for collateral valuation under CER-POL-001 §6.2, and feed the stressed LGD of section 4.6.

sections.heading: Mortgage module – affordability PD uplift
sections.text: The affordability channel is estimated with a logistic regression of the 12-month default indicator on the energy-cost-to-income ratio (ECTI), lagged by six months, controlling for the PD-MORT-NL score, indexed LTV, loan-to-income and year fixed effects, on the affordability panel. Household energy expenditure is estimated per loan from the label class, dwelling type and floor area using the CBS and RVO energy consumption tables, multiplied by the prevailing gas and electricity tariffs; the economic rationale is that higher energy costs reduce the income available for debt service. The ECTI coefficient is 0.082 (standard error 0.019, p < 0.001): an increase of one percentage point in ECTI multiplies the odds of default by 1.085, a positive sign consistent with the 2022 episode. Variables tested and rejected were the label class itself (collinear with ECTI and not significant in its presence, p = 0.41) and regional gas network dependency, which is not available in production. Under a scenario, the projected ECTI per loan determines a PD multiplier relative to the starting point, applied to the point-in-time PD of the IFRS 9 mortgage model for credit losses and to the IRB PD for RWA, after the macro uplift of MDL-10. Under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario, the peak (2028) PD multipliers are 1.29 for label G, 1.21 for F, 1.14 for E, 1.08 for D, 1.04 for C and 1.02 for B and better; the exposure-weighted portfolio multiplier is 1.07. The energy efficiency of the collateral is thereby reflected together with the debt service capacity of the borrower.

The ECTI coefficient is 0.082 (standard error 0.019, p < 0.001): an increase of one percentage point in ECTI multiplies the odds of default by 1.085, a positive sign consistent with the 2022 episode. Variables tested and rejected were the label class itself (collinear with ECTI and not significant in its presence, p = 0.41) and regional gas network dependency, which is not available in production.

sections.heading: Corporate module – sector mapping and carbon cost
sections.text: Obligors are mapped to 22 transition-risk sectors via the mapping table CTR-MAP-NACE v1.2 (RDS §4.1.4). For each obligor and scenario year, the direct carbon cost is computed as Scope 1 emissions (plus Scope 2 for sectors without full electricity cost pass-through and Scope 3 for oil and gas, automotive and chemicals) multiplied by the scenario carbon price, net of free allocation under the EU ETS until its phase-out for CBAM sectors in 2034. The share of the carbon cost passed on to customers is set per sector by the expert panel (EJ-CTR-04): utilities 70%, oil and gas 60%, road freight 50%, chemicals 45%, cement 40%, iron and steel 35% and livestock farming 20%. Demand effects are taken from the NGFS sectoral gross value added paths, and transition capex from sector investment needs aligned with the IEA Net Zero pathway where the obligor has not published a transition plan. Obligors are classified as directly exposed (Scope 1 intensity above 500 t CO2e per EUR million revenue) or indirectly exposed (material Scope 3 emissions or dependence on fossil fuel demand), and this classification is written back as a climate risk indicator to the credit review file, where it is assessed at origination and at each annual review.

sections.heading: Corporate module – financial projection and rating migration
sections.text: For the 250 bottom-up obligors (71% of drawn exposure in transition-sensitive sectors), EBITDA, interest coverage, net debt/EBITDA and solvency are projected per scenario year by applying the net carbon cost, the demand effect and capex financing to the latest financial statements. The projected ratios are scored with the financial module of the MDL-06 corporate rating scorecard (weights and bins unchanged), the qualitative module is held constant, and the change in score is mapped to notches on the Bank's master scale with a maximum of four notches per year. The resulting grade is translated into a point-in-time PD with the IFRS 9 corporate PD term structure for credit losses and into the IRB PD of the grade for RWA, so that rating migration feeds through to risk-weighted assets as a second-round effect. For the remaining obligors, sector PD multipliers are derived from the bottom-up results per sector and scenario year, scaled by the ratio of sector emission intensities, and capped at 3.0. Under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario the peak (2029) PD multipliers are: oil and gas extraction 2.6, cement and lime 2.2, fossil power generation 1.9, iron and steel 2.0, chemicals 1.7, livestock farming 1.6, road freight 1.5 and 1.05 or lower for low-carbon sectors; the exposure-weighted multiplier for transition-sensitive sectors is 1.46.

sections.heading: LGD and EAD treatment
sections.text: Mortgage LGD is recomputed with the production LGD model (MDL-02) using the label-differentiated stressed collateral values; under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario the exposure-weighted stressed LGD rises from 11.4% to 12.6%, and to 15.9% for label G. For corporates, recoveries on collateral of obligors in fossil fuel extraction and fossil power generation are reduced by stranded-asset haircuts of 35% and 25% respectively (EJ-CTR-07), while the LGD of unsecured exposures is unchanged. EAD includes undrawn commitments with the CCFs of the IRB models, and a scenario-dependent additional drawdown of 10 percentage points is applied to revolving facilities of obligors downgraded by two or more notches. LGD and EAD are applied as point-in-time values for credit losses and as downturn values for RWA. The credit risk analysis therefore covers the borrower's ability to repay (PD), recoveries including the deterioration of collateral values (LGD), and the size and dynamics of exposure including undrawn commitments (EAD).

sections.heading: Portfolio alignment metrics
sections.text: In addition to risk parameters, CTR computes forward-looking alignment metrics for transition planning: for power generation, oil and gas, cement, steel and automotive, the exposure-weighted emission intensity of the portfolio is compared with the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 sector pathways (2023 update), with base year 2022 and 89% exposure coverage in these sectors. For mortgages, the metric is the label distribution and the average primary energy use (kWh per m2) of the collateral, compared with a national pathway consistent with the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU) 2024/1275. The choice of pathways, base year and sectors was approved by the Enterprise Risk Committee on 3 February 2027; sectors are selected where the Bank's exposure exceeds EUR 250 million and a recognised pathway exists, and any change is documented and justified. Alignment gaps are monitored at least annually against the milestones of the prudential transition plan; at 31 December 2026 the power generation portfolio was 18% above the pathway intensity for 2026, and the share of F and G labels in the mortgage book was 12.9% against a milestone of 12.5%. The metrics support the quantified targets and intermediate milestones of the Bank's prudential transition plan, which is kept consistent with its sustainability disclosures, and the financial implications of the plan are assessed with the long-term scenario results of section 7.5.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: Carbon prices, energy prices and sectoral output are taken from the NGFS database for the EU region and for the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany; household gas and electricity tariffs are derived from wholesale prices with the historical pass-through estimated on CBS tariff data 2015–2025 (elasticity 0.71). Carbon prices are converted from USD 2010 to EUR 2024 with the ECB reference exchange rate and the euro area HICP. NGFS variables are not applied mechanistically: the short-term scenario uses the NGFS narrative and variable shocks rescaled to the ICAAP adverse macroeconomic paths, so that GDP and unemployment in CTR-ST-ADV equal the ICAAP adverse values of MDL-10 in each year, and the long-term variables are disaggregated to the Bank's three countries and 22 sectors. Scenario values outside the historical range (EU carbon prices above EUR 105 per tonne were never observed) are handled through the structural present-value formula of section 4.2 and the ratio projections of section 4.5; extrapolation was tested up to EUR 800 per tonne and is monotonic without explosive results, with the PD cap of 3.0 applied to sector multipliers. The calibration of the scenario layer is therefore customised to the objective, scope and granularity of the analysis and to the risk characteristics of the Bank's portfolios.

sections.heading: Translation into risk parameters
sections.text: The stressed PD for exposure i in year t is PD_it = min(0.999; PD_it,macro × M_it), where PD_it,macro is the point-in-time PD under the macroeconomic scenario from the IFRS 9 models and MDL-10, and M_it the CTR multiplier from section 4.3 (mortgages) or 4.5 (corporates). Multipliers are applied on the odds scale for mortgages and through the rating scale for bottom-up corporates, which keeps the stressed PDs internally consistent with the master scale. Stressed LGD and EAD are computed as in section 4.6; all parameters are annual and mutually consistent because they use the same scenario variables and the same macroeconomic base. The translation of scenario variables into PD and LGD shocks relies on expert judgement for the pass-through rates, the renovation costs and the stranded-asset haircuts, which is documented in chapter 11 and approved under MRM-STD-023. The formulas, parameter values and code references in this section and in chapter 4 allow Model Validation to reproduce the estimation and calibration without recourse to the developers.

sections.heading: Aggregation to losses, RWA and capital
sections.text: The stressed parameters are loaded into the Bank's stress testing platform, which computes per year the incremental credit losses (IFRS 9 provisions under the stressed point-in-time parameters), risk-weighted exposure amounts via the IRB formula after rating migration, the foregone interest on defaulted exposures, and the own funds and CET1 ratio impact. Results are broken down by portfolio, label class, sector and country, and reported before and after management actions; the only management action considered is the reduction of new lending to fossil fuel extraction already embedded in the sector policy, which is feasible within the scenario and implemented within twelve months, with an impact of 3 bp on the CET1 ratio. The ICAAP climate results are combined with the ICAAP adverse scenario without diversification: the climate increment is added to the credit losses and RWA of the adverse scenario. The Bank thus defines its own climate scenario capturing its material vulnerabilities, instead of relying on supervisory stress test scenarios, and translates it into risk, loss and capital figures in both ICAAP perspectives.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: A margin of conservatism under CRM-STD-101 is not applicable, because CTR is not an IRB model; the heading is retained in line with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. Uncertainty is instead addressed through two documented conservative adjustments on model results: +5% on mortgage module losses and RWA for the uncertainty from estimated energy labels (EJ-CTR-06, deficiencies DD-CTR-02 and DD-CTR-03), and +10% on corporate module losses for unmodelled value-chain effects and tipping points (EJ-CTR-09). The +5% mortgage adjustment was set as the midpoint between zero and the +6.2% sensitivity obtained by shifting all estimated labels one class worse (section 7.4), which is regarded as a conservative upper bound of the estimation error. Together the adjustments add EUR 32 million to the ICAAP climate adverse losses (7.7% of the climate increment of EUR 418 million), are included in all reported results, and will be presented with the approval request. Limitations of CTR used in the ICAAP are thereby reflected through documented adjustments, in line with ERM-STD-300 §9.3. Each adjustment addresses a specific limitation (L-03 and L-07), is reassessed semi-annually with the monitoring cycle, and is planned to be removed when registered label coverage reaches 75% of exposure (target December 2028) and when value-chain effects are modelled in version 2.0 (target ICAAP 2029).

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: As no climate-related loss history exists, CTR components will be back-tested against the closest historical analogue, the 2022–2023 energy price shock. The mortgage back-test on the June 2022 portfolio has been completed: the affordability model predicted an increase in inflows into 3–6 months arrears of 9.4% for labels E–G against a realised increase of 7.1%. The corporate back-test on the 2021 financial statements of obligors in energy-intensive sectors and the back-test of the hedonic projection are in progress and will be reported in version 1.0.

evidence.quote: The mortgage back-test on the June 2022 portfolio has been completed: the affordability model predicted an increase in inflows into 3–6 months arrears of 9.4% for labels E–G against a realised increase of 7.1%.

sections.heading: Out-of-sample and out-of-time performance
sections.text: The affordability model has an AUC of 0.861 on the development sample, 0.858 out-of-sample and 0.849 out-of-time (2023–2024); the ECTI coefficient estimated on the out-of-time period alone is 0.076, within the 95% confidence interval of the development estimate. The calibration of the affordability model is accurate on the out-of-time sample (Jeffreys test p = 0.38 at portfolio level). The hedonic model explains 81% of the variance of log prices out-of-time (2024–2025), with label coefficients stable within ±0.6 percentage points between 2022 and 2025. The corporate migration mapping reproduces the realised out-of-time (2022–2025) one-year migration matrix with a mean absolute difference of 0.9 percentage points per cell, and the projected grades have a Gini of 0.71 for one-year default prediction. Performance is reported for each segment: per label group for the affordability model (AUC between 0.832 for labels A–C and 0.866 for F–G) and per sector group for the migration mapping. The migration mapping for agriculture (Gini 0.52) is below the internal expectation of 0.60; the cause (few rated obligors and the dominance of regulatory shocks such as the nitrogen measures) was analysed, recorded as limitation L-08 and addressed by a conservative sector-level calibration. Metrics and thresholds follow MV-HB-003 where applicable to the component (discriminatory power, calibration and stability).

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: Alternative A (top-down sector multipliers from NGFS gross value added through the MDL-10 corporate satellite) is maintained as challenger for the corporate module; under CTR-ST-ADV it produces incremental corporate losses of EUR 231 million against EUR 287 million for CTR (−20%). The difference is explained by obligor-level emissions: the challenger assigns sector averages, whereas 34 of the bottom-up obligors have emission intensities more than twice their sector average; CTR is retained because it captures this concentration. The mortgage module is benchmarked against a label-bucket approach based on the published methodology of the ECB 2022 climate risk stress test, which yields EUR 118 million against EUR 131 million for CTR, and the interim approach (economic add-on of EUR 190 million) serves as benchmark for the economic perspective (CTR: EUR 236 million). The champion–challenger difference of 20% is reported to the Stress Testing Steering Committee as the measure of model uncertainty under the adverse scenario. The calibration was also compared with the sector results published in supervisory climate exercises and with the outcome of the sensitivity analyses in section 7.4; no third-party model is used, so no supplier validation framework needed to be verified.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivities were computed on the ICAAP climate adverse scenario at the reference date 31 December 2026, with total incremental losses of EUR 418 million. Carbon price +50%: +31%; carbon cost pass-through rates −20 percentage points: +19%; estimated labels shifted one class worse: mortgage losses +6.2%; capitalisation rate 0.30 instead of 0.46: mortgage losses −9%; ECTI coefficient at the lower bound of its 95% confidence interval: mortgage losses −18%; stranded-asset haircuts ±10 percentage points: corporate losses ±3.4%; exclusion of 2015 from the affordability panel: +0.9%; exclusion of imputed records: −0.6%. Results are most sensitive to the carbon price and the pass-through rates, which are therefore set conservatively within the expert panel range (lower quartile of pass-through) and disclosed with the results. The sensitivity to each material expert judgement (EJ-CTR-04, -05, -06, -07 and -09) is recorded in the EJ log together with the alternative values considered. Non-linearities were examined by doubling the carbon price shock: losses increase by a factor of 2.3, reflecting the rating migration thresholds and the PD cap.

sections.heading: Results of the 2026 dry run
sections.text: The dry run on the reference date 31 December 2026 (run CTR-DR-2026Q4-03 of 28 April 2027) produced the following results. ICAAP normative perspective, CTR-ST-ADV compared with the ICAAP adverse scenario without climate drivers: cumulative incremental credit losses 2027–2029 of EUR 418 million (mortgages EUR 131 million, corporates EUR 287 million), incremental RWA of EUR 2.9 billion in 2029 and a further reduction of the CET1 ratio at the trough (2029) of 78 bp, of which 33 bp from losses and 45 bp from RWA migration. ICAAP economic perspective: climate transition internal capital add-on of EUR 236 million at the reference date. Long term, Delayed Transition: expected loss of the mortgage portfolio rises from 3.1 bp to 5.0 bp in 2035, concentrated in labels E–G, and that of transition-sensitive corporate sectors from 38 bp to 71 bp; under Net Zero 2050 the corresponding 2035 values are 3.9 bp and 52 bp, and under Current Policies 3.2 bp and 41 bp. Of the corporate increment, 61% arises from five sectors representing 14% of drawn exposure, which confirms the sectoral concentration identified in the materiality assessment and supports the sector concentration limits.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (1) the energy-cost channel observed in 2022 is representative of future carbon-price-driven energy cost shocks; (2) house prices capitalise 46% of the present value of energy and renovation cost differences; (3) the corporate rating scorecard remains valid for projected financial ratios outside the historical range; (4) pass-through rates are constant over the horizon; (5) the balance sheet is static, with maturing exposures replaced by exposures of the same label or sector; (6) physical and transition risks are additive. Each assumption was assessed for plausibility: (1) and (2) are supported by the back-tests in chapter 7, (3) by the extrapolation tests in chapter 5, and (4) to (6) are simplifications whose effects are covered by the sensitivities in section 7.4 and by the conservative adjustment EJ-CTR-09. Methodological uncertainty specific to climate risk arises from the long horizons, the absence of historical climate-related loss data and the dependence of results on scenario assumptions such as the carbon price path; long-term results are therefore reported as ranges across scenarios and sensitivities rather than as point estimates. The exclusion of physical risk from CTR is justified by the separate physical risk assessment of Sustainability Risk; compound effects of simultaneous physical and transition shocks are not captured beyond additive aggregation (limitation L-09). Climate risks are not excluded because they are difficult to quantify: where data are lacking, plausible assumptions and proxies are used and documented, and their uncertainty is reflected in conservative adjustments.

sections.heading: Limitations log
sections.text: The limitations log of CTR contains nine entries, each with identifier, description, source, estimated impact, mitigating measure and owner; material limitations will be reported to the approval authority at gate G3 and recorded in the model inventory. L-01 No loss-based back-testing (source: absence of climate loss history; impact not quantifiable; mitigation: analogue back-tests and ex-post comparison of first-year projections; owner: Model Owner). L-02 Static balance sheet (source: design choice; impact −4% to +6% on long-term EL; mitigation: dynamic sensitivity in the resilience analysis; owner: Enterprise Stress Testing). L-03 Estimated energy labels for 34.9% of mortgage exposure (source: DD-CTR-01 to DD-CTR-03; impact +6.2% on mortgage losses if one class worse; mitigation: adjustment EJ-CTR-06 and label coverage programme; owner: ESG Data Lead). L-04 Constant pass-through rates (source: expert judgement; impact ±19%; mitigation: sensitivity reporting; owner: Model Owner). L-05 Proxied emissions for 36.9% of corporate exposure (source: DD-CTR-05; impact ±8% on corporate losses; mitigation: PCAF score monitoring and reported data from the 2027 CSRD cycle; owner: Sustainability Risk Modelling). L-06 Sector misclassification of holding companies (source: DD-CTR-04; impact 1.8%; mitigation: re-mapping EJ-CTR-02). L-07 Value-chain and tipping-point effects not modelled (impact not quantifiable; mitigation: adjustment EJ-CTR-09). L-08 Weaker migration mapping for agriculture (Gini 0.52; mitigation: conservative sector calibration). L-09 Compound physical and transition effects not modelled (mitigation: additive aggregation and qualitative assessment; owner: Sustainability Risk). The log is complete, kept up to date with each model version and provided to users with the results.

sections.heading: Use of results and communication to the management body
sections.text: Each CTR results pack submitted to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and, as part of the ICAAP, to the Management Board contains the scenario narratives, the key assumptions, an extract of the limitations log, the champion–challenger range and the conservative adjustments, so that the management body can challenge the key modelling assumptions and the scenario selection. Approximations in the results (sector proxies, estimated labels and the additive combination with physical risk) are explained in the results pack together with the evidence of chapter 7 on their reliability for ICAAP capital planning. The results are used in ICAAP capital planning and in setting the climate key risk indicators of the risk appetite statement (the fossil fuel sector limit and the share of F and G labels in new mortgage production), which are monitored quarterly, as well as in the materiality assessment and the prudential transition plan. Known limitations and conditions of use are recorded in the model inventory and communicated to all users with each results pack. The Management Board approves the annual stress testing programme, including the climate stress test (programme 2027 approved on 16 December 2026), and was involved in the definition of the ICAAP adverse scenario, including its climate overlay, on 20 January 2027. The climate stress test is part of the risk management framework and the ICAAP, and its results support strategic and capital planning, taking the limitations above into account.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: CTR is implemented as a climate module of the Bank's stress testing platform (STP), which already hosts the MDL-10 satellites. The implementation specification CTR-IS v1.0, approved by the Model Owner on 2 April 2027 before implementation started and consistent with this MDD, defines for every input variable the production source field and lineage, and every transformation, missing value and outlier treatment, formula, parameter table, cap and rounding convention. The handover package delivered to the STP development team on 6 April 2027 contains the specification, the parameter tables (label haircuts, ECTI coefficient, pass-through rates, sector multipliers and stranded-asset haircuts), 186 test cases with expected outputs produced with the development code, and reference outputs for the full portfolio of 31 December 2026. The test cases cover typical cases, boundary values (label A++++ and G, carbon price 0 and 800), missing and invalid inputs, and every label class, sector and country. Implementation testing, reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing are reported in EVD-19-ITR.

sections.heading: Production controls
sections.text: Development and production code are held in the Bank's GitLab; production runs in STP use the tagged release ctr-stp-1.0.0 and the parameter set CTR-PAR-1.0, and each run logs the reference date, input data version, code version and parameter set. Parameter tables are version controlled, access is restricted to the STP administrators, and changes are made only through change management; model developers have read-only access to the production environment. Changes to production code require a four-eyes review by a person other than the author and approval by the Model Owner before deployment; emergency changes require the approval of the Model Owner and MRM, and outstanding tests are completed within 30 calendar days. Manual reruns and manual adjustments of outputs are permitted only with a ticket approved by the Head of Enterprise Stress Testing and are logged in the run log; the conservative adjustments of chapter 6 are implemented as parameters, not as manual adjustments. ICAAP results are retained with the input data and the code version used to produce them for at least ten years.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: A monitoring plan will be prepared before go-live in accordance with MRM-STD-040. Candidate KPIs are the registered label coverage of mortgage exposure, the share of corporate exposure with proxied emissions, the PSI of the label and sector distribution, the ex-post deviation of baseline projections and the champion–challenger difference. Thresholds, frequency and responsibilities are still to be agreed with Model Risk Management.

sections.heading: Annual review, ex-post comparison and re-validation triggers
sections.text: Climate stress testing with CTR is performed at least annually, as part of the ICAAP and the internal climate stress test. After each ICAAP cycle, the baseline first-year projection of arrears, downgrades and losses in the transition-sensitive segments is compared with realised outcomes, and material deviations are analysed and reported to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and, with the ICAAP review, to senior management. The annual model review by the Model Owner covers monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes (including new NGFS scenario vintages and climate policy changes such as the emissions trading system for buildings and road transport), open findings and data deficiencies, the EJ log and the conservative adjustments, and code–documentation consistency; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose and whether action is required, and is signed off by the Model Owner and submitted to MRM. The appropriateness of the data sources and methods of CTR is thereby evaluated in a regular internal review, and scenarios and narratives are reviewed annually by Enterprise Stress Testing and Sustainability Risk and whenever significant changes in the business environment occur. The Model Owner confirms the consistency between production code, implementation specification and MDD after each change and at least annually. The contribution of CTR to the effectiveness of the stress testing programme is assessed annually in the programme review of Enterprise Stress Testing, using quantitative evidence (ex-post comparison, challenger differences) and qualitative feedback from the Stress Testing Steering Committee. A re-validation is triggered by an unresolved red monitoring outcome, a material change in portfolio composition or in the climate policy environment, a relevant regulatory change or a change in intended use.

sections.heading: Expert judgement
sections.text: All expert judgements in CTR are recorded in the EJ log CTR-EJ v1.2, stored with the model documentation; the log contains nine entries (EJ-CTR-01 to EJ-CTR-09), three in data treatment (RDS documentation chapter 9) and six in model design and calibration. Model design and calibration judgements are: EJ-CTR-04 carbon cost pass-through rates per sector (high materiality; a change of 20 percentage points changes corporate losses by 19%); EJ-CTR-05 renovation cost per label step (medium); EJ-CTR-06 +5% mortgage adjustment for estimated labels (medium); EJ-CTR-07 stranded-asset haircuts (medium, ±3.4%); EJ-CTR-08 country disaggregation of energy prices (low); EJ-CTR-09 +10% corporate adjustment for value-chain effects (medium). Each entry records the type, life-cycle stage and affected parameter, the rationale with the evidence relied on (for EJ-CTR-04: the empirical literature on cost pass-through in the EU ETS, sector studies and the expert panel of 12 March and 2 April 2027), the alternatives considered and rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver and approval date, and the review date and expiry condition. EJ-CTR-04 was elicited from an expert panel whose composition, Delphi elicitation method, individual contributions and aggregation by median are documented in the panel minutes (EVD-19-EJP). Medium-materiality judgements were approved by the Model Owner and the Head of Risk Modelling after documented challenge by the climate risk officer of Sustainability Risk (2LoD); the high-materiality judgement EJ-CTR-04 will be submitted to the Model Risk Committee after review by Model Validation; no proposer is the sole approver of a judgement. Judgements whose impact cannot be quantified, such as EJ-CTR-09, are classified at least as medium materiality; the design judgements (forced inclusion of label source as control variable, reference class and functional form of the haircut) are justified in chapter 4.

sections.heading: Model change governance
sections.text: Changes to CTR after approval will be recorded in the change log of the model inventory before implementation and documented in a change memorandum that describes the change and its rationale, the affected components and documents, the internal materiality classification with its analysis, the quantitative impact, the required validation and the implementation plan. A change is internally material if it alters the methodology, the risk drivers, the scenario set used for the ICAAP, the range of application or the use, introduces a new material data source, or changes the ICAAP climate losses or the economic add-on at the latest reference date by more than 5% or moves more than 10% of exposures between label or sector groups. The classification proposed by the developer is approved by MRM, disagreements are escalated to the MRC, and the higher class is applied where the classification is uncertain. Related changes, such as a new NGFS scenario vintage together with the recalibration of pass-through rates, are assessed as a single change; changes are not split to avoid a higher classification, and the cumulative impact since the last full validation is tracked and determines whether the next validation is full scope. Material changes are independently validated before implementation and pass gates G1 to G4; non-material changes are approved by the Model Owner after MRM has confirmed the classification, the new version is recorded in the inventory, and a post-implementation review of each material change compares realised and estimated impact within six months and is reported to MRM.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: CTR quantifies the impact of climate transition risk on the credit risk of the Bank's Dutch residential mortgage portfolio and of its corporate lending portfolio in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Its primary uses are (a) the climate component of the ICAAP normative adverse scenario over 2027–2029, (b) the internal capital add-on for climate transition risk in the ICAAP economic perspective, and (c) the annual internal climate stress test with long-term scenario analysis to 2050 under ERM-STD-300 §10 and EBA/GL/2025/04. Secondary uses are the quantitative input to the annual C&E materiality assessment (CER-POL-001 §5), the forward-looking metrics of the prudential transition plan and the calibration of sector concentration thresholds by Credit Risk Management. CTR is not used for own funds requirements, IFRS 9 expected credit loss, pricing or individual credit decisions. Users are Enterprise Stress Testing (execution of runs), Capital Management (ICAAP), Sustainability Risk (materiality assessment) and Credit Risk Management (sector policies). The purpose of each analysis is defined in advance: the short-term analysis tests capital adequacy, the long-term analysis tests the resilience of the business model, and neither is a forecast; the expectations and limitations of each analysis are stated with its results (section 8.3).

sections.heading: Regulatory context and applicable requirements
sections.text: CTR implements CER-POL-001 §7–§11 and ERM-STD-300 §10, and addresses EBA/GL/2025/01, EBA/GL/2025/04, the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks (Expectations 7, 8 and 11) and the ECB Guide to the ICAAP (Principles 3, 6 and 7). The applicable requirement set was derived from the Bank's requirement library at the start of development (requirement set RS-MDL19-01 of 2 October 2026) and was used to plan the evidence and the structure of this MDD and of the RDS documentation. CTR is a quantitative method whose output is used for risk measurement and reporting; it is therefore a model under MRM-POL-001 and is managed across the full model lifecycle, developed under MRM-STD-020 and documented under MRM-STD-021. The model was assessed against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act: CTR is estimated with classical econometric methods (ordinary least squares and logistic regression) and applied as fixed, documented equations with expert-calibrated parameters, and in line with the Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system it is assessed as not being an AI system; this conclusion was recorded in the model inventory on 21 September 2026, before gate G1.

sections.heading: Model inventory record and tiering
sections.text: A model identification questionnaire (MIQ-2026-044) was submitted to MRM on 1 September 2026, and MRM concluded on 18 September 2026, within 20 business days, that CTR is a model and recorded the rationale. CTR was registered in the model inventory under identifier MDL-19 on 21 September 2026 (gate G0), before development started; version 1.0 is the version described in this document. The inventory record states the model name, version, purpose, intended and secondary uses, scope of application (Dutch residential mortgages and corporate lending in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany), risk type (climate transition risk as a driver of credit risk), regulatory use (ICAAP and stress testing) and model family (statistical). The model owner is M. de Groot, Head of Sustainability Risk Modelling, a 1LoD senior manager who remains accountable for the tasks delegated to the lead developer; the developers are the Sustainability Risk Modelling team, the main users Enterprise Stress Testing and Capital Management, and the assigned validation team Model Validation – Enterprise Risk. The model owner proposed the tier with the tiering template, scoring materiality High on criterion (a), since the portfolios covered exceed EUR 10 billion, and complexity High (scenario-based methodology, dependencies on five other models, extensive expert judgement). MRM recorded a provisional Tier 2 on 21 September 2026 on the basis that the model produces a Pillar 2 add-on rather than own funds requirements; the tier is provisional until confirmed at the first validation. As a model used for ICAAP and stress testing, CTR is in any case at least Tier 2 under MRM-STD-010 §6.5. The inventory record also states the AI Act classification (not an AI system), the personal data indicator (yes) and the DPIA reference DPIA-2026-118-A2. The model owner updates the inventory record within ten business days of any change to a mandatory attribute and at each gate, and attests the record quarterly (last attestation 31 March 2027).

sections.heading: Lifecycle status and governance
sections.text: CTR is in the development stage: gate G0 was passed on 21 September 2026 and gate G1 (development sign-off) is planned for 25 June 2027, after completion of the 1LoD self-assessment against RS-MDL19-01. No gate is passed before the preceding gates are complete, and each gate decision and its evidence are recorded in the model inventory. After G1 the model will be submitted to Model Validation – Enterprise Risk for a full-scope initial validation (G2, planned July–September 2027); approval for use (G3) lies with the Model Approval Panel, whose decision is reported to the MRC at its next meeting, and go-live (G4) is planned for November 2027, before the 2027 climate stress test and the ICAAP 2028 cycle. The model will be validated independently before first use and after every material change, and periodically at least every two years as a Tier 2 model, counted from the previous validation opinion. The validators assigned to CTR have not contributed to its development; an Enterprise Stress Testing modeller who moved to Model Validation in January 2026 and contributed to the scenario design has been excluded from the validation team. CTR will not be used with a Not fit for purpose opinion, and any conditions attached to a Fit for purpose with conditions opinion will be recorded in the MRC conditions register with an owner and a deadline. For every open high- or medium-severity finding, the model owner will submit a remediation plan within 20 business days of the final validation report. The approval request will contain the validation opinion, the 1LoD self-assessment, open findings, known limitations and the conservative adjustments of chapter 6. Until CTR is approved, the ICAAP continues to use the interim expert-based climate add-on of EUR 190 million, approved by the Enterprise Risk Committee on 14 March 2026.

sections.heading: Link to the materiality assessment and the ICAAP risk inventory
sections.text: The 2026 C&E materiality assessment of Sustainability Risk, performed annually and updated on material changes and approved by the Management Board on 15 December 2026, concluded that transition risk is material for credit risk in the mortgage portfolio (labels E–G) and in six corporate sector groups over the medium and long term, and not material for market and liquidity risk given the Bank's limited trading book and the composition of its liquidity buffer. The assessment covered transition and physical risk drivers and their impact on credit, market, operational, liquidity, reputational and business model risk, and combined exposure-based methods (sector and label concentrations), portfolio-based methods (alignment metrics) and scenario-based methods (the 2025 interim climate stress test). Materiality thresholds were 5% of CET1 capital for cumulative losses over the medium term and 1% of total exposure for concentrations; each non-materiality conclusion is documented with the evidence and threshold applied. The outcome feeds the ICAAP risk inventory, in which climate transition risk was recorded as a driver of credit risk in the annual risk identification exercise of March 2027, the stress testing programme and the model development plan, which triggered the development of CTR. The measurement approach is commensurate with the materiality outcome: material portfolios are modelled at exposure level, while non-material portfolios (SME retail and consumer lending) are covered by sector proxies in the materiality assessment only, and CTR outputs in turn feed the next materiality assessment. A gap analysis of the Bank's stress testing models by Enterprise Stress Testing (October 2026) found that the credit satellites of MDL-10 contain no environment-sensitive variables; CTR addresses this structurally rather than through ad hoc adjustments, starting with credit risk, and the extension to the banking book bond portfolio and to operational risk is planned for 2028–2029.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: CTR consists of a scenario layer and two portfolio modules, linked to the Bank's existing credit risk parameter models. The scenario layer translates NGFS Phase V long-term and NGFS short-term scenario variables (carbon prices, energy prices, sectoral gross value added and household energy expenditure) for the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany into the model's risk drivers, consistently with the macroeconomic paths of MDL-10. The mortgage module projects label-differentiated house prices and energy-cost affordability shocks per loan and converts them into PD multipliers (via the energy-cost-to-income ratio) and stressed LGD (via indexed LTV). The corporate module projects carbon costs, pass-through, demand effects and transition capex at obligor level for the 250 largest obligors in transition-sensitive sectors (bottom-up) and at sector level for the remaining obligors, which are grouped by transition-risk sector and country, and converts the projections into rating migrations and point-in-time PDs. Both modules produce stressed PD, LGD and EAD per exposure and year, which the stress testing platform aggregates into incremental credit losses, risk-weighted assets and CET1 impact. Segmentation is by label class (eight classes) and dwelling type for mortgages and by 22 transition-risk sectors and three countries for corporates.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: CTR depends on the following approved models: MDL-10 Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (macro paths and macro-driven PD and LGD satellites), the production versions of MDL-01 (PD residential mortgages) and MDL-02 (LGD residential mortgages) for loan-level starting parameters, MDL-06 PD Corporates (financial scorecard and master scale used for rating migration), and the production versions of MDL-07 and MDL-08 (IFRS 9 point-in-time PD term structures). The risk parameters to which CTR applies its climate multipliers are thus produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001. CTR adds only the climate-differentiated component on top of these models: the same satellite model (MDL-10) is used for the macro-driven PD component in stress testing, IFRS 9 and ICAAP, and CTR does not re-estimate macro sensitivities, so that the climate increment is not double counted. The purpose-driven difference is that CTR applies its multipliers to point-in-time PDs for credit losses and to the IRB PD after rating migration for risk-weighted assets (section 5.3). Changes to an upstream model are notified to the CTR model owner through the dependency register of the inventory and trigger an impact assessment under MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Scenario set and narratives
sections.text: The scenario set combines a short-term ICAAP scenario and three long-term scenarios, all based on recognised reference pathways, and is used to test the Bank's resilience to climate risk under different scenarios. Short term (2027–2029): the ICAAP climate adverse scenario CTR-ST-ADV overlays the NGFS short-term 'Sudden Wake-Up Call' narrative, in which an abrupt tightening of climate policy triggers a sharp repricing of carbon-intensive activities, on the Bank's ICAAP 2027 adverse macroeconomic scenario; the EU carbon price rises from EUR 78 per tonne CO2e (2026 average) to EUR 190 in 2028 and EUR 240 in 2029, and household gas tariffs increase by 45% in 2028. The ICAAP baseline embeds the NGFS Current Policies trajectory, consistent with the Bank's reference scenario (common narrative of the most likely evolution of the business environment), which the Management Board endorsed on 10 December 2026 and which is used across business planning and the ICAAP. Long term (2027–2050): NGFS Phase V Net Zero 2050 (orderly transition), Delayed Transition (disorderly transition) and Current Policies (hot house world), with EU carbon prices of EUR 185, 85 and 90 per tonne in 2030 and EUR 350, 480 and 95 in 2040 respectively (EUR 2024 prices). Each scenario has a written narrative, approved by the Stress Testing Steering Committee on 18 January 2027, describing the triggering events and the transmission to energy prices, sectoral output, household budgets and house prices; the quantified paths were checked for consistency with the narrative. Physical risk is not modelled in CTR; for the hot house world scenario, the physical risk impact on collateral is added at aggregation level from the Sustainability Risk physical risk assessment, and this exclusion from the CTR narrative is justified in section 8.1. The same NGFS scenario families are used for the ICAAP, the prudential transition plan and the materiality assessment, and the selection of scenarios and any change to it are documented and justified in the annual scenario review.

sections.heading: Scenario severity and consistency
sections.text: The severity of CTR-ST-ADV was calibrated against historical and hypothetical events: the 2028 household energy cost shock corresponds to 70% of the peak increase of Dutch household gas tariffs in 2022, and the two-year carbon price increase corresponds to the 97.5th percentile of two-year changes across the NGFS Phase V scenario ensemble and exceeds the largest two-year increase observed in the EU ETS (2021–2022). Consistency between variables is ensured by taking energy prices, GDP and sectoral gross value added from the same NGFS model run, and by applying the ICAAP adverse macroeconomic paths of MDL-10 unchanged. Expert adjustments to scenario paths are limited to the disaggregation of EU energy prices to the three countries (EJ-CTR-08), which is documented and approved under MRM-STD-023. The ICAAP adverse scenario covers GDP, unemployment, residential and commercial real estate prices, the interest rate term structure, credit spreads, equity prices, exchange rates and inflation; CTR adds carbon prices, household and industrial energy prices and sectoral output to this set. The combined scenario is severe but plausible: it reflects the Bank's material vulnerabilities identified in the risk identification process (concentrations in Dutch residential real estate and in energy-intensive sectors) and reduces the CET1 ratio at the trough by a further 78 bp in addition to the ICAAP adverse scenario, consistent with its purpose of testing capital adequacy.

sections.heading: Transmission channels and mitigating factors
sections.text: The transmission channels were identified in a structured process with Sustainability Risk, Credit Risk Management and Economic Research (workshops of 3 and 17 November 2026), building on the 2026 materiality assessment, and are reviewed annually together with the materiality assessment. Mortgages: (M1) energy-label-driven changes in collateral values through the capitalisation of higher energy and renovation costs; (M2) energy-cost-driven deterioration of borrower affordability; (M3) renovation financing needs increasing indebtedness, which is assessed qualitatively. Corporates: (C1) carbon-price-driven costs reducing profitability, net of pass-through to customers; (C2) demand shifts in sectors facing substitution, such as fossil fuels and internal combustion vehicles; (C3) transition capital expenditure increasing leverage; (C4) stranded-asset risk reducing collateral recoveries in fossil fuel sectors. Physical risk channels (flood and subsidence damage to collateral) are covered by the physical risk assessment of Sustainability Risk and not by CTR; within CTR the channels are mapped to credit risk (default probabilities and collateral values) only. Mitigating and amplifying factors are included where material within the horizon: announced corporate transition plans reduce the carbon cost only where capex is committed and financed (credited for 41 of the 250 bottom-up obligors); national subsidies for home insulation reduce renovation costs by 20% in the orderly scenario only; and no additional government support is assumed in the disorderly scenarios.

sections.heading: Time horizons and capital perspectives
sections.text: CTR produces results for three horizons consistent with CER-POL-001 §5.3: short term (2027–2029, the three-year ICAAP normative horizon), medium term (to 2035) and long term (to 2050, in five-year steps). In the normative perspective, the stressed PD, LGD and RWA feed the three-year projection of own funds and capital ratios under the ICAAP baseline and adverse scenarios, which are updated with every ICAAP cycle. In the economic perspective, CTR provides a point-in-time add-on at the reference date, defined as the difference between the credit risk economic capital computed with climate-adjusted point-in-time PDs and LGDs (Delayed Transition calibration of the first projection year) and the unadjusted economic capital, complemented by a medium-term view of the add-on to 2035. The long-term results support the resilience analysis of the business model required by EBA/GL/2025/04, projecting expected loss and the risk-adjusted margin of the in-scope portfolios over more than ten years, and are not translated into capital figures. Climate risk is treated as a driver of credit risk; no diversification benefit between climate and other credit risk drivers is assumed, and gross figures are reported.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: Model development uses the frozen RDS RDS-CTR-2026Q4 v1.0, approved on 12 March 2027 (EVD-19-RDS), whose construction, representativeness and data quality are documented there. Samples were defined before estimation: for the affordability model, the development sample covers 2015–2022 (random 70% of loans), the out-of-sample test the remaining 30% of loans and the out-of-time sample 2023–2024; for the hedonic model, development covers 2019–2023 and out-of-time 2024–2025; for the corporate migration mapping, development covers 2014–2021 and out-of-time 2022–2025. Out-of-time samples were not used for variable selection or parameter estimation. Candidate variables were assessed for economic rationale, availability in the production data of the stress testing platform and stability over the observation period; the label method (EL_METHOD) and label source (registered or estimated) are retained as control variables. The data limitations (estimated labels, proxied emissions) are carried into the limitations log (section 8.2) and into the conservative adjustments (chapter 6).

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Three methodological alternatives were assessed against documented criteria: regulatory expectations, data availability, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation in the stress testing platform. (A) Top-down sector multipliers: PD multipliers per sector derived from NGFS sectoral gross value added through the MDL-10 corporate satellite; simple and transparent, but insensitive to obligor-level emissions and pass-through. (B) Bottom-up financial projection with rating migration for large obligors and label-level mortgage shocks, combined with sector multipliers for the remaining obligors; sensitive to exposure-level emissions and labels and interpretable, but data intensive. (C) Structural climate-adjusted Merton model with asset value shocks from discounted carbon costs; theoretically coherent, but dependent on equity data that are unavailable for 83% of obligors and difficult to reconcile with the Bank's rating scale. Alternative B was selected because it applies shocks at exposure level where data permit, reflects obligor emissions and energy labels, reuses the approved rating scorecard and master scale, and passed the back-tests in section 7.1; alternative A is retained as challenger model (section 7.3). The selected approach relies on transparent regression and scorecard mechanics, so no transparency is traded for performance, and it is tailored to the Bank's business model and portfolios rather than imported from an external methodology.

sections.heading: Mortgage module – energy label house price differentials
sections.text: The collateral channel is based on a hedonic regression of the logarithm of transaction prices on energy label dummies (reference class B), dwelling characteristics (floor area, type, construction period and plot size), municipality-by-quarter fixed effects and the label method, estimated per year on the hedonic sample. The estimated price differential of label G relative to label B widened from −3.1% in 2019 to −7.8% in 2024, with a marked increase after the 2022 energy price shock, which supports the capitalisation of energy costs into prices. Under a scenario, the additional label differential is projected as the present value of the scenario increase in annual energy costs and of the renovation cost to reach label B, multiplied by the estimated capitalisation rate of 0.46, the share of that present value reflected in prices according to the 2021–2024 change in differentials. The resulting peak house price haircuts relative to label C, applied on top of the MDL-10 house price index path, are: label A and better +1.0%, B 0.0%, D −3.5%, E −6.0%, F −9.0% and G −12.5% under Delayed Transition (peak in 2035), and 60% of these values under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario by 2029. Label C is the reference class because its price path is closest to the national house price index; the exposure-weighted portfolio haircut is −2.0%. Stressed indexed collateral values therefore reflect the energy label of each property, as required for collateral valuation under CER-POL-001 §6.2, and feed the stressed LGD of section 4.6.

sections.heading: Mortgage module – affordability PD uplift
sections.text: The affordability channel is estimated with a logistic regression of the 12-month default indicator on the energy-cost-to-income ratio (ECTI), lagged by six months, controlling for the PD-MORT-NL score, indexed LTV, loan-to-income and year fixed effects, on the affordability panel. Household energy expenditure is estimated per loan from the label class, dwelling type and floor area using the CBS and RVO energy consumption tables, multiplied by the prevailing gas and electricity tariffs; the economic rationale is that higher energy costs reduce the income available for debt service. The ECTI coefficient is 0.082 (standard error 0.019, p < 0.001): an increase of one percentage point in ECTI multiplies the odds of default by 1.085, a positive sign consistent with the 2022 episode. Variables tested and rejected were the label class itself (collinear with ECTI and not significant in its presence, p = 0.41) and regional gas network dependency, which is not available in production. Under a scenario, the projected ECTI per loan determines a PD multiplier relative to the starting point, applied to the point-in-time PD of the IFRS 9 mortgage model for credit losses and to the IRB PD for RWA, after the macro uplift of MDL-10. Under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario, the peak (2028) PD multipliers are 1.29 for label G, 1.21 for F, 1.14 for E, 1.08 for D, 1.04 for C and 1.02 for B and better; the exposure-weighted portfolio multiplier is 1.07. The energy efficiency of the collateral is thereby reflected together with the debt service capacity of the borrower.

sections.heading: Corporate module – sector mapping and carbon cost
sections.text: Obligors are mapped to 22 transition-risk sectors via the mapping table CTR-MAP-NACE v1.2 (RDS §4.1.4). For each obligor and scenario year, the direct carbon cost is computed as Scope 1 emissions (plus Scope 2 for sectors without full electricity cost pass-through and Scope 3 for oil and gas, automotive and chemicals) multiplied by the scenario carbon price, net of free allocation under the EU ETS until its phase-out for CBAM sectors in 2034. The share of the carbon cost passed on to customers is set per sector by the expert panel (EJ-CTR-04): utilities 70%, oil and gas 60%, road freight 50%, chemicals 45%, cement 40%, iron and steel 35% and livestock farming 20%. Demand effects are taken from the NGFS sectoral gross value added paths, and transition capex from sector investment needs aligned with the IEA Net Zero pathway where the obligor has not published a transition plan. Obligors are classified as directly exposed (Scope 1 intensity above 500 t CO2e per EUR million revenue) or indirectly exposed (material Scope 3 emissions or dependence on fossil fuel demand), and this classification is written back as a climate risk indicator to the credit review file, where it is assessed at origination and at each annual review.

sections.heading: Corporate module – financial projection and rating migration
sections.text: For the 250 bottom-up obligors (71% of drawn exposure in transition-sensitive sectors), EBITDA, interest coverage, net debt/EBITDA and solvency are projected per scenario year by applying the net carbon cost, the demand effect and capex financing to the latest financial statements. The projected ratios are scored with the financial module of the MDL-06 corporate rating scorecard (weights and bins unchanged), the qualitative module is held constant, and the change in score is mapped to notches on the Bank's master scale with a maximum of four notches per year. The resulting grade is translated into a point-in-time PD with the IFRS 9 corporate PD term structure for credit losses and into the IRB PD of the grade for RWA, so that rating migration feeds through to risk-weighted assets as a second-round effect. For the remaining obligors, sector PD multipliers are derived from the bottom-up results per sector and scenario year, scaled by the ratio of sector emission intensities, and capped at 3.0. Under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario the peak (2029) PD multipliers are: oil and gas extraction 2.6, cement and lime 2.2, fossil power generation 1.9, iron and steel 2.0, chemicals 1.7, livestock farming 1.6, road freight 1.5 and 1.05 or lower for low-carbon sectors; the exposure-weighted multiplier for transition-sensitive sectors is 1.46.

sections.heading: LGD and EAD treatment
sections.text: Mortgage LGD is recomputed with the production LGD model (MDL-02) using the label-differentiated stressed collateral values; under the ICAAP climate adverse scenario the exposure-weighted stressed LGD rises from 11.4% to 12.6%, and to 15.9% for label G. For corporates, recoveries on collateral of obligors in fossil fuel extraction and fossil power generation are reduced by stranded-asset haircuts of 35% and 25% respectively (EJ-CTR-07), while the LGD of unsecured exposures is unchanged. EAD includes undrawn commitments with the CCFs of the IRB models, and a scenario-dependent additional drawdown of 10 percentage points is applied to revolving facilities of obligors downgraded by two or more notches. LGD and EAD are applied as point-in-time values for credit losses and as downturn values for RWA. The credit risk analysis therefore covers the borrower's ability to repay (PD), recoveries including the deterioration of collateral values (LGD), and the size and dynamics of exposure including undrawn commitments (EAD).

sections.heading: Portfolio alignment metrics
sections.text: In addition to risk parameters, CTR computes forward-looking alignment metrics for transition planning: for power generation, oil and gas, cement, steel and automotive, the exposure-weighted emission intensity of the portfolio is compared with the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 sector pathways (2023 update), with base year 2022 and 89% exposure coverage in these sectors. For mortgages, the metric is the label distribution and the average primary energy use (kWh per m2) of the collateral, compared with a national pathway consistent with the recast Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU) 2024/1275. The choice of pathways, base year and sectors was approved by the Enterprise Risk Committee on 3 February 2027; sectors are selected where the Bank's exposure exceeds EUR 250 million and a recognised pathway exists, and any change is documented and justified. Alignment gaps are monitored at least annually against the milestones of the prudential transition plan; at 31 December 2026 the power generation portfolio was 18% above the pathway intensity for 2026, and the share of F and G labels in the mortgage book was 12.9% against a milestone of 12.5%. The metrics support the quantified targets and intermediate milestones of the Bank's prudential transition plan, which is kept consistent with its sustainability disclosures, and the financial implications of the plan are assessed with the long-term scenario results of section 7.5.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: Carbon prices, energy prices and sectoral output are taken from the NGFS database for the EU region and for the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany; household gas and electricity tariffs are derived from wholesale prices with the historical pass-through estimated on CBS tariff data 2015–2025 (elasticity 0.71). Carbon prices are converted from USD 2010 to EUR 2024 with the ECB reference exchange rate and the euro area HICP. NGFS variables are not applied mechanistically: the short-term scenario uses the NGFS narrative and variable shocks rescaled to the ICAAP adverse macroeconomic paths, so that GDP and unemployment in CTR-ST-ADV equal the ICAAP adverse values of MDL-10 in each year, and the long-term variables are disaggregated to the Bank's three countries and 22 sectors. Scenario values outside the historical range (EU carbon prices above EUR 105 per tonne were never observed) are handled through the structural present-value formula of section 4.2 and the ratio projections of section 4.5; extrapolation was tested up to EUR 800 per tonne and is monotonic without explosive results, with the PD cap of 3.0 applied to sector multipliers. The calibration of the scenario layer is therefore customised to the objective, scope and granularity of the analysis and to the risk characteristics of the Bank's portfolios.

The calibration of the scenario layer is therefore customised to the objective, scope and granularity of the analysis and to the risk characteristics of the Bank's portfolios.

sections.heading: Translation into risk parameters
sections.text: The stressed PD for exposure i in year t is PD_it = min(0.999; PD_it,macro × M_it), where PD_it,macro is the point-in-time PD under the macroeconomic scenario from the IFRS 9 models and MDL-10, and M_it the CTR multiplier from section 4.3 (mortgages) or 4.5 (corporates). Multipliers are applied on the odds scale for mortgages and through the rating scale for bottom-up corporates, which keeps the stressed PDs internally consistent with the master scale. Stressed LGD and EAD are computed as in section 4.6; all parameters are annual and mutually consistent because they use the same scenario variables and the same macroeconomic base. The translation of scenario variables into PD and LGD shocks relies on expert judgement for the pass-through rates, the renovation costs and the stranded-asset haircuts, which is documented in chapter 11 and approved under MRM-STD-023. The formulas, parameter values and code references in this section and in chapter 4 allow Model Validation to reproduce the estimation and calibration without recourse to the developers.
