sections.heading: Aggregation to losses, RWA and capital
sections.text: The stressed parameters are loaded into the Bank's stress testing platform, which computes per year the incremental credit losses (IFRS 9 provisions under the stressed point-in-time parameters), risk-weighted exposure amounts via the IRB formula after rating migration, the foregone interest on defaulted exposures, and the own funds and CET1 ratio impact. Results are broken down by portfolio, label class, sector and country, and reported before and after management actions; the only management action considered is the reduction of new lending to fossil fuel extraction already embedded in the sector policy, which is feasible within the scenario and implemented within twelve months, with an impact of 3 bp on the CET1 ratio. The ICAAP climate results are combined with the ICAAP adverse scenario without diversification: the climate increment is added to the credit losses and RWA of the adverse scenario. The Bank thus defines its own climate scenario capturing its material vulnerabilities, instead of relying on supervisory stress test scenarios, and translates it into risk, loss and capital figures in both ICAAP perspectives.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: A margin of conservatism under CRM-STD-101 is not applicable, because CTR is not an IRB model; the heading is retained in line with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. Uncertainty is instead addressed through two documented conservative adjustments on model results: +5% on mortgage module losses and RWA for the uncertainty from estimated energy labels (EJ-CTR-06, deficiencies DD-CTR-02 and DD-CTR-03), and +10% on corporate module losses for unmodelled value-chain effects and tipping points (EJ-CTR-09). The +5% mortgage adjustment was set as the midpoint between zero and the +6.2% sensitivity obtained by shifting all estimated labels one class worse (section 7.4), which is regarded as a conservative upper bound of the estimation error. Together the adjustments add EUR 32 million to the ICAAP climate adverse losses (7.7% of the climate increment of EUR 418 million), are included in all reported results, and will be presented with the approval request. Limitations of CTR used in the ICAAP are thereby reflected through documented adjustments, in line with ERM-STD-300 §9.3. Each adjustment addresses a specific limitation (L-03 and L-07), is reassessed semi-annually with the monitoring cycle, and is planned to be removed when registered label coverage reaches 75% of exposure (target December 2028) and when value-chain effects are modelled in version 2.0 (target ICAAP 2029).

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: As no climate-related loss history exists, CTR components are back-tested against the closest historical analogue, the 2022–2023 energy price shock. Mortgage module: applying the realised 2022 household energy tariffs to the June 2022 portfolio, the affordability model predicted an increase in inflows into 3–6 months arrears of 9.4% for labels E–G against a realised increase of 7.1%, and of 2.2% against 1.8% for labels A–C, i.e. directionally correct and moderately conservative. Corporate module: applying the realised 2022 gas and carbon prices to the 2021 financial statements of 96 obligors in energy-intensive sectors, the bottom-up projection predicted a downgrade of at least one notch for 17 obligors against 14 realised downgrades, with 12 obligors in both groups. The hedonic projection of label differentials was back-tested on 2023–2024: the model calibrated on 2019–2022 predicted a widening of the G-versus-B differential to −6.9% against the estimated −7.8%. The back-tests validate the key assumptions and parameters of the transmission channels; the absence of loss-based back-testing is recorded as limitation L-01, and qualitative assessment by the expert panel and benchmarking complement the quantitative evidence.

sections.heading: Out-of-sample and out-of-time performance
sections.text: The affordability model has an AUC of 0.861 on the development sample, 0.858 out-of-sample and 0.849 out-of-time (2023–2024); the ECTI coefficient estimated on the out-of-time period alone is 0.076, within the 95% confidence interval of the development estimate. The calibration of the affordability model is accurate on the out-of-time sample (Jeffreys test p = 0.38 at portfolio level). The hedonic model explains 81% of the variance of log prices out-of-time (2024–2025), with label coefficients stable within ±0.6 percentage points between 2022 and 2025. The corporate migration mapping reproduces the realised out-of-time (2022–2025) one-year migration matrix with a mean absolute difference of 0.9 percentage points per cell, and the projected grades have a Gini of 0.71 for one-year default prediction. Performance is reported for each segment: per label group for the affordability model (AUC between 0.832 for labels A–C and 0.866 for F–G) and per sector group for the migration mapping. The migration mapping for agriculture (Gini 0.52) is below the internal expectation of 0.60; the cause (few rated obligors and the dominance of regulatory shocks such as the nitrogen measures) was analysed, recorded as limitation L-08 and addressed by a conservative sector-level calibration. Metrics and thresholds follow MV-HB-003 where applicable to the component (discriminatory power, calibration and stability).

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: Alternative A (top-down sector multipliers from NGFS gross value added through the MDL-10 corporate satellite) is maintained as challenger for the corporate module; under CTR-ST-ADV it produces incremental corporate losses of EUR 231 million against EUR 287 million for CTR (−20%). The difference is explained by obligor-level emissions: the challenger assigns sector averages, whereas 34 of the bottom-up obligors have emission intensities more than twice their sector average; CTR is retained because it captures this concentration. The mortgage module is benchmarked against a label-bucket approach based on the published methodology of the ECB 2022 climate risk stress test, which yields EUR 118 million against EUR 131 million for CTR, and the interim approach (economic add-on of EUR 190 million) serves as benchmark for the economic perspective (CTR: EUR 236 million). The champion–challenger difference of 20% is reported to the Stress Testing Steering Committee as the measure of model uncertainty under the adverse scenario. The calibration was also compared with the sector results published in supervisory climate exercises and with the outcome of the sensitivity analyses in section 7.4; no third-party model is used, so no supplier validation framework needed to be verified.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivities were computed on the ICAAP climate adverse scenario at the reference date 31 December 2026, with total incremental losses of EUR 418 million. Carbon price +50%: +31%; carbon cost pass-through rates −20 percentage points: +19%; estimated labels shifted one class worse: mortgage losses +6.2%; capitalisation rate 0.30 instead of 0.46: mortgage losses −9%; ECTI coefficient at the lower bound of its 95% confidence interval: mortgage losses −18%; stranded-asset haircuts ±10 percentage points: corporate losses ±3.4%; exclusion of 2015 from the affordability panel: +0.9%; exclusion of imputed records: −0.6%. Results are most sensitive to the carbon price and the pass-through rates, which are therefore set conservatively within the expert panel range (lower quartile of pass-through) and disclosed with the results. The sensitivity to each material expert judgement (EJ-CTR-04, -05, -06, -07 and -09) is recorded in the EJ log together with the alternative values considered. Non-linearities were examined by doubling the carbon price shock: losses increase by a factor of 2.3, reflecting the rating migration thresholds and the PD cap.

sections.heading: Results of the 2026 dry run
sections.text: The dry run on the reference date 31 December 2026 (run CTR-DR-2026Q4-03 of 28 April 2027) produced the following results. ICAAP normative perspective, CTR-ST-ADV compared with the ICAAP adverse scenario without climate drivers: cumulative incremental credit losses 2027–2029 of EUR 418 million (mortgages EUR 131 million, corporates EUR 287 million), incremental RWA of EUR 2.9 billion in 2029 and a further reduction of the CET1 ratio at the trough (2029) of 78 bp, of which 33 bp from losses and 45 bp from RWA migration. ICAAP economic perspective: climate transition internal capital add-on of EUR 236 million at the reference date. Long term, Delayed Transition: expected loss of the mortgage portfolio rises from 3.1 bp to 5.0 bp in 2035, concentrated in labels E–G, and that of transition-sensitive corporate sectors from 38 bp to 71 bp; under Net Zero 2050 the corresponding 2035 values are 3.9 bp and 52 bp, and under Current Policies 3.2 bp and 41 bp. Of the corporate increment, 61% arises from five sectors representing 14% of drawn exposure, which confirms the sectoral concentration identified in the materiality assessment and supports the sector concentration limits.

sections.heading: Use in reverse stress testing
sections.text: In the 2027 reverse stress test, Enterprise Stress Testing used CTR to determine the climate shock that, combined with the ICAAP adverse scenario, would lead to a breach of the total SREP capital requirement. The breach would require an EU carbon price of EUR 1,150 per tonne by 2029 combined with a 60% increase in household gas tariffs, which the Stress Testing Steering Committee assessed as implausible within a three-year horizon. The result was used to confirm the severity of CTR-ST-ADV and to challenge the fossil fuel sector limit of the risk appetite statement, which was lowered from EUR 1.2 billion to EUR 1.0 billion.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (1) the energy-cost channel observed in 2022 is representative of future carbon-price-driven energy cost shocks; (2) house prices capitalise 46% of the present value of energy and renovation cost differences; (3) the corporate rating scorecard remains valid for projected financial ratios outside the historical range; (4) pass-through rates are constant over the horizon; (5) the balance sheet is static, with maturing exposures replaced by exposures of the same label or sector; (6) physical and transition risks are additive. Each assumption was assessed for plausibility: (1) and (2) are supported by the back-tests in chapter 7, (3) by the extrapolation tests in chapter 5, and (4) to (6) are simplifications whose effects are covered by the sensitivities in section 7.4 and by the conservative adjustment EJ-CTR-09. Methodological uncertainty specific to climate risk arises from the long horizons, the absence of historical climate-related loss data and the dependence of results on scenario assumptions such as the carbon price path; long-term results are therefore reported as ranges across scenarios and sensitivities rather than as point estimates. The exclusion of physical risk from CTR is justified by the separate physical risk assessment of Sustainability Risk; compound effects of simultaneous physical and transition shocks are not captured beyond additive aggregation (limitation L-09). Climate risks are not excluded because they are difficult to quantify: where data are lacking, plausible assumptions and proxies are used and documented, and their uncertainty is reflected in conservative adjustments.

sections.heading: Limitations log
sections.text: The limitations log of CTR contains nine entries, each with identifier, description, source, estimated impact, mitigating measure and owner; material limitations will be reported to the approval authority at gate G3 and recorded in the model inventory. L-01 No loss-based back-testing (source: absence of climate loss history; impact not quantifiable; mitigation: analogue back-tests and ex-post comparison of first-year projections; owner: Model Owner). L-02 Static balance sheet (source: design choice; impact −4% to +6% on long-term EL; mitigation: dynamic sensitivity in the resilience analysis; owner: Enterprise Stress Testing). L-03 Estimated energy labels for 34.9% of mortgage exposure (source: DD-CTR-01 to DD-CTR-03; impact +6.2% on mortgage losses if one class worse; mitigation: adjustment EJ-CTR-06 and label coverage programme; owner: ESG Data Lead). L-04 Constant pass-through rates (source: expert judgement; impact ±19%; mitigation: sensitivity reporting; owner: Model Owner). L-05 Proxied emissions for 36.9% of corporate exposure (source: DD-CTR-05; impact ±8% on corporate losses; mitigation: PCAF score monitoring and reported data from the 2027 CSRD cycle; owner: Sustainability Risk Modelling). L-06 Sector misclassification of holding companies (source: DD-CTR-04; impact 1.8%; mitigation: re-mapping EJ-CTR-02). L-07 Value-chain and tipping-point effects not modelled (impact not quantifiable; mitigation: adjustment EJ-CTR-09). L-08 Weaker migration mapping for agriculture (Gini 0.52; mitigation: conservative sector calibration). L-09 Compound physical and transition effects not modelled (mitigation: additive aggregation and qualitative assessment; owner: Sustainability Risk). The log is complete, kept up to date with each model version and provided to users with the results.

sections.heading: Use of results and communication to the management body
sections.text: Each CTR results pack submitted to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and, as part of the ICAAP, to the Management Board contains the scenario narratives, the key assumptions, an extract of the limitations log, the champion–challenger range and the conservative adjustments, so that the management body can challenge the key modelling assumptions and the scenario selection. Approximations in the results (sector proxies, estimated labels and the additive combination with physical risk) are explained in the results pack together with the evidence of chapter 7 on their reliability for ICAAP capital planning. The results are used in ICAAP capital planning and in setting the climate key risk indicators of the risk appetite statement (the fossil fuel sector limit and the share of F and G labels in new mortgage production), which are monitored quarterly, as well as in the materiality assessment and the prudential transition plan. Known limitations and conditions of use are recorded in the model inventory and communicated to all users with each results pack. The Management Board approves the annual stress testing programme, including the climate stress test (programme 2027 approved on 16 December 2026), and was involved in the definition of the ICAAP adverse scenario, including its climate overlay, on 20 January 2027. The climate stress test is part of the risk management framework and the ICAAP, and its results support strategic and capital planning, taking the limitations above into account.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: CTR is implemented as a climate module of the Bank's stress testing platform (STP), which already hosts the MDL-10 satellites. The implementation specification CTR-IS v1.0, approved by the Model Owner on 2 April 2027 before implementation started and consistent with this MDD, defines for every input variable the production source field and lineage, and every transformation, missing value and outlier treatment, formula, parameter table, cap and rounding convention. The handover package delivered to the STP development team on 6 April 2027 contains the specification, the parameter tables (label haircuts, ECTI coefficient, pass-through rates, sector multipliers and stranded-asset haircuts), 186 test cases with expected outputs produced with the development code, and reference outputs for the full portfolio of 31 December 2026. The test cases cover typical cases, boundary values (label A++++ and G, carbon price 0 and 800), missing and invalid inputs, and every label class, sector and country. Implementation testing, reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing are reported in EVD-19-ITR.

sections.heading: Production controls
sections.text: Development and production code are held in the Bank's GitLab; production runs in STP use the tagged release ctr-stp-1.0.0 and the parameter set CTR-PAR-1.0, and each run logs the reference date, input data version, code version and parameter set. Parameter tables are version controlled, access is restricted to the STP administrators, and changes are made only through change management; model developers have read-only access to the production environment. Changes to production code require a four-eyes review by a person other than the author and approval by the Model Owner before deployment; emergency changes require the approval of the Model Owner and MRM, and outstanding tests are completed within 30 calendar days. Manual reruns and manual adjustments of outputs are permitted only with a ticket approved by the Head of Enterprise Stress Testing and are logged in the run log; the conservative adjustments of chapter 6 are implemented as parameters, not as manual adjustments. ICAAP results are retained with the input data and the code version used to produce them for at least ten years.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-CTR v1.0, approved by the Model Owner on 28 May 2027 and to be reviewed by Model Validation during the initial validation, defines KPIs equivalent to discriminatory power and calibration, since a scenario model cannot be monitored against realised defaults in the usual way. KPIs and green/amber/red thresholds are: registered label coverage of mortgage exposure (≥65% / 55–65% / <55%); share of corporate exposure with PCAF score 4–5 (≤40% / 40–50% / >50%); PSI of the label and sector distribution against the development portfolio (<0.10 / 0.10–0.25 / >0.25); relative deviation of the baseline first-year projection from realised arrears and downgrades in transition-sensitive segments (≤25% / 25–50% / >50%); champion–challenger difference (≤25% / 25–40% / >40%); and share of in-scope exposure without CTR output (≤1% / 1–3% / >3%). The thresholds were approved by Model Risk Management on 2 June 2027. KPIs are computed for the overall model and for each module, label group and sector group, semi-annually and at each ICAAP run, with results finalised within 60 calendar days of the reference date by Sustainability Risk Modelling and reported to the Model Owner, Enterprise Stress Testing and Credit Risk Management. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed within 60 calendar days by a root cause analysis and an action plan proposing no action with justification, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use, with changes processed under MRM-STD-050. The monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over at least the last four cycles, lists the conservative adjustments in force with amount, purpose and planned removal date, and shows model coverage. Monitoring code is held in the ctr-climate repository (tag mon-v1.0.0) and results are reproducible; the plan is updated whenever the model changes and reviewed at least annually.

sections.heading: Annual review, ex-post comparison and re-validation triggers
sections.text: Climate stress testing with CTR is performed at least annually, as part of the ICAAP and the internal climate stress test. After each ICAAP cycle, the baseline first-year projection of arrears, downgrades and losses in the transition-sensitive segments is compared with realised outcomes, and material deviations are analysed and reported to the Stress Testing Steering Committee and, with the ICAAP review, to senior management. The annual model review by the Model Owner covers monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes (including new NGFS scenario vintages and climate policy changes such as the emissions trading system for buildings and road transport), open findings and data deficiencies, the EJ log and the conservative adjustments, and code–documentation consistency; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose and whether action is required, and is signed off by the Model Owner and submitted to MRM. The appropriateness of the data sources and methods of CTR is thereby evaluated in a regular internal review, and scenarios and narratives are reviewed annually by Enterprise Stress Testing and Sustainability Risk and whenever significant changes in the business environment occur. The Model Owner confirms the consistency between production code, implementation specification and MDD after each change and at least annually. The contribution of CTR to the effectiveness of the stress testing programme is assessed annually in the programme review of Enterprise Stress Testing, using quantitative evidence (ex-post comparison, challenger differences) and qualitative feedback from the Stress Testing Steering Committee. A re-validation is triggered by an unresolved red monitoring outcome, a material change in portfolio composition or in the climate policy environment, a relevant regulatory change or a change in intended use.

sections.heading: Expert judgement
sections.text: All expert judgements in CTR are recorded in the EJ log CTR-EJ v1.2, stored with the model documentation; the log contains nine entries (EJ-CTR-01 to EJ-CTR-09), three in data treatment (RDS documentation chapter 9) and six in model design and calibration. Model design and calibration judgements are: EJ-CTR-04 carbon cost pass-through rates per sector (high materiality; a change of 20 percentage points changes corporate losses by 19%); EJ-CTR-05 renovation cost per label step (medium); EJ-CTR-06 +5% mortgage adjustment for estimated labels (medium); EJ-CTR-07 stranded-asset haircuts (medium, ±3.4%); EJ-CTR-08 country disaggregation of energy prices (low); EJ-CTR-09 +10% corporate adjustment for value-chain effects (medium). Each entry records the type, life-cycle stage and affected parameter, the rationale with the evidence relied on (for EJ-CTR-04: the empirical literature on cost pass-through in the EU ETS, sector studies and the expert panel of 12 March and 2 April 2027), the alternatives considered and rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver and approval date, and the review date and expiry condition. EJ-CTR-04 was elicited from an expert panel whose composition, Delphi elicitation method, individual contributions and aggregation by median are documented in the panel minutes (EVD-19-EJP). Medium-materiality judgements were approved by the Model Owner and the Head of Risk Modelling after documented challenge by the climate risk officer of Sustainability Risk (2LoD); the high-materiality judgement EJ-CTR-04 will be submitted to the Model Risk Committee after review by Model Validation; no proposer is the sole approver of a judgement. Judgements whose impact cannot be quantified, such as EJ-CTR-09, are classified at least as medium materiality; the design judgements (forced inclusion of label source as control variable, reference class and functional form of the haircut) are justified in chapter 4.

sections.heading: Aggregate effect of expert judgement and overlays
sections.text: The aggregate effect of all expert judgements on the ICAAP climate adverse result was quantified by re-running the model with the best statistical or neutral alternative for each judgement (panel median pass-through, no adjustments, sector-average renovation costs): the aggregate effect is +14.6% of the incremental losses (EUR 61 million). Because the aggregate effect exceeds the 5% high-materiality threshold of MRM-STD-023 §4.2, the aggregate will be submitted to the Model Risk Committee for approval together with the G3 approval request, although the approval authority for the model itself is the Model Approval Panel. The two conservative adjustments (EJ-CTR-06 and EJ-CTR-09) are overlays in the sense of MRM-STD-023 §3.5: each addresses a specific limitation, is quantified by a documented method and has a removal plan with target date. An overlay that remains in place for more than 24 months will trigger a model change assessment under MRM-STD-050. Each expert judgement is reviewed at each annual model review and whenever new data could replace it, and withdrawn judgements are kept in the log.

sections.heading: Model change governance
sections.text: Changes to CTR after approval will be recorded in the change log of the model inventory before implementation and documented in a change memorandum that describes the change and its rationale, the affected components and documents, the internal materiality classification with its analysis, the quantitative impact, the required validation and the implementation plan. A change is internally material if it alters the methodology, the risk drivers, the scenario set used for the ICAAP, the range of application or the use, introduces a new material data source, or changes the ICAAP climate losses or the economic add-on at the latest reference date by more than 5% or moves more than 10% of exposures between label or sector groups. The classification proposed by the developer is approved by MRM, disagreements are escalated to the MRC, and the higher class is applied where the classification is uncertain. Related changes, such as a new NGFS scenario vintage together with the recalibration of pass-through rates, are assessed as a single change; changes are not split to avoid a higher classification, and the cumulative impact since the last full validation is tracked and determines whether the next validation is full scope. Material changes are independently validated before implementation and pass gates G1 to G4; non-material changes are approved by the Model Owner after MRM has confirmed the classification, the new version is recorded in the inventory, and a post-implementation review of each material change compares realised and estimated impact within six months and is reported to MRM.

documents.title: Climate transition risk data quality assessment report (RDS-CTR-2026Q4)

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the candidate reference data set RDS-CTR-2026Q4 v1.0 of the Climate Transition Risk model (MDL-19), performed from 1 to 23 February 2027 under MRM-STD-022 §5.1 before model development. The assessment covers the 47 critical data elements (CDEs) and 126 DQ rules of rule book DQR-CTR v1.0, on the four mandatory dimensions (completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness) and, where relevant, validity, uniqueness and appropriateness. It was performed by the CTR development team together with the Data Stewards of the five data domains, and the rules were executed in the Group DQ monitoring tool (rule set DQM-CTR-01) on the candidate RDS and on the production input data of the 31 December 2026 dry run. Report version 1.0; author T. Mulder (Modeller, Sustainability Risk Modelling); reviewer R. Janssen; approved by the Model Owner on 26 February 2027.

sections.heading: Results per dimension
sections.text: Completeness: 45 of 47 CDEs green; obligor revenue is amber (97.9% non-missing against the 98% amber threshold, caused by newly onboarded holding entities), and the registered energy label is green against its model-specific threshold (65.1% of exposure against amber 60%). Accuracy: all 29 accuracy rules green; the largest reconciliation difference is 0.08% of corporate drawn exposure, explained by accrued interest. Consistency: 30 of 31 rules green; the rule 'NACE code consistent with the reported revenue split' is amber (98.6% of records passing against the 99% amber threshold) because of holding companies, which are re-mapped in the RDS build. Timeliness: 18 of 19 rules green; the age of the latest financial statement exceeds 18 months for 6.4% of corporate obligors, which is amber. No red result was observed on any CDE, and the results per rule, variable and dimension against their thresholds are listed in Annex 1 of this report.

sections.heading: Sample-based verification against source documentation
sections.text: A sample of 300 properties, stratified by label class and label source, was verified against the EP-Online register and the valuation report in the credit file; label agreement was 99.3%. A sample of 120 corporate obligors, stratified by sector and emissions source, was verified against the emissions published in sustainability statements or annual reports; 7 obligors (5.8%) showed differences above 10% because the vendor used the prior reporting year, and the difference was recorded as DD-CTR-05. For 60 estimated labels, a desk review of the building characteristics confirmed the plausibility of the estimate in 52 cases; in 6 of the remaining 8 cases the estimate was too favourable, which is consistent with the bias recorded in DD-CTR-03. The verification was performed by two developers and documented with the file references of each checked item.

sections.heading: Energy label coverage monitoring
sections.text: Energy label coverage and quality have been monitored quarterly in the ESG data quality dashboard since the first quarter of 2026. The share of mortgage exposure with a registered label was 61.8% in Q1, 62.9% in Q2, 64.0% in Q3 and 65.1% in Q4 2026; the share with an estimated label decreased correspondingly from 38.2% to 34.9%. The share of registered labels is 71.4% for loans originated after 2021 and 58.2% for older loans, because a label is registered at every property transaction. Coverage is reported per portfolio (owner-occupied mortgages only, as CTR does not cover buy-to-let or commercial real estate) to the Sustainability Risk function and in the quarterly data quality report to the Model Owner.

sections.heading: Emissions data quality
sections.text: The exposure-weighted PCAF data quality score of corporate emissions is 3.4; by exposure, 12.1% has score 1–2 (verified or unverified reported emissions), 22.1% score 3 (reported emissions without verification or physical-activity based), 28.9% score 4 (vendor estimates based on production or revenue) and 36.9% score 5 (PCAF sector averages). The ESG data platform identifies, collects and structures the emissions data and stores the source and score of each value, and the quarterly DQ report tracks the score distribution to measure the improvement expected from the first CSRD reporting cycles. Vendor data are assessed for fitness for use at each delivery: the delivery of 30 November 2026 covered 71% of the requested obligors, with 41% of the vendor values based on sector-average intensities. The data quality score of each estimate is carried into the RDS so that the model results can be broken down by data quality.

documents.title: Expert panel minutes – climate transmission calibration

sections.heading: Purpose and mandate of the panel
sections.text: The expert panel was convened by the Model Owner of CTR (MDL-19) to elicit three calibration inputs for which no sufficient statistical evidence exists: the carbon cost pass-through rates per sector (EJ-CTR-04), the stranded-asset haircuts on collateral in fossil fuel sectors (EJ-CTR-07) and the renovation cost per label step (EJ-CTR-05). The mandate, approved by the Model Owner on 20 February 2027, requires the panel to document its composition, the elicitation method, the individual contributions and the aggregation, in line with MRM-STD-023 §2.6. These minutes are the evidence referenced in the CTR expert judgement log and in MDD chapter 11.

sections.heading: Panel composition and independence
sections.text: The panel consisted of seven experts: two sector specialists of Credit Risk Management (energy and utilities; industry and materials), one agricultural lending specialist, one economist of Economic Research, one modeller of Enterprise Stress Testing, one real estate valuation expert of the collateral management department, and one modeller of Sustainability Risk Modelling who did not develop the calibration code. The CTR lead developer acted as facilitator without voting rights. The climate risk officer of Sustainability Risk (2LoD) attended as independent challenger and did not contribute estimates. No panel member has objectives linked to the size of the CTR add-on.

sections.heading: Elicitation method
sections.text: A two-round Delphi method was used. In round 1 (12 March 2027), each expert received an evidence pack (empirical studies of cost pass-through under the EU ETS, sector margin data 2015–2025, the 2022 energy crisis experience in the Bank's portfolio and the NGFS sector output paths) and submitted individual estimates with a lower bound, a best estimate and an upper bound, together with a written rationale. In round 2 (2 April 2027), the anonymised distribution of round 1 estimates and rationales was shared and experts could revise their estimates. The aggregate is the median of the round 2 best estimates; the interquartile range is recorded as the uncertainty range, and the lower quartile is used where conservatism requires lower pass-through. The rationale of each expert is recorded in Annex 1, so that a third party can understand the basis of each estimate and replicate the aggregation.

sections.heading: Pass-through rates – individual contributions and results
sections.text: Round 2 best estimates of the pass-through rate for cement were 30%, 35%, 40%, 40%, 45%, 50% and 55% (median 40%, interquartile range 35–50%); for iron and steel 25%, 30%, 35%, 35%, 40%, 45% and 50% (median 35%). For utilities the median was 75% with an interquartile range of 65–80%, for oil and gas 60% (55–70%), for road freight 55% (45–60%), for chemicals 45% (40–55%) and for livestock farming 20% (10–25%); all individual contributions per sector and round are listed in Annex 1. The panel agreed to use the median for most sectors and, for utilities and road freight, a value five percentage points below the median (70% and 50%) to reflect the risk of lower pass-through in a disorderly transition. The dispersion narrowed between rounds for all sectors, with the largest remaining disagreement for livestock farming, where the outcome depends on national nitrogen policy.

sections.heading: Stranded-asset haircuts
sections.text: The stranded-asset haircuts were discussed in a plenary session on 2 April 2027 on the basis of the recovery experience on coal-related collateral in 2016–2021 and the remaining economic life of gas-fired plants under the Delayed Transition scenario. The panel reached consensus on haircuts of 35% for collateral of fossil fuel extraction obligors and 25% for fossil power generation. The consensus values were recorded; individual estimates were not collected for this item because the discussion converged quickly. The sensitivity of ±10 percentage points changes corporate losses by ±3.4% and is reported in MDD §7.4.

sections.heading: Renovation costs and conservatism for hard-to-quantify effects
sections.text: The renovation cost per label step (for example EUR 44,000 from label G to label B for a terraced house of 110 m2, in 2026 prices) was derived from the RVO reference measures and contractor price data and confirmed by the valuation expert, who adjusted the costs for apartments by −15%. For effects that are hard to quantify, notably value-chain disruption and tipping points in carbon-intensive sectors, the panel recommended a conservative adjustment rather than exclusion, and proposed the +10% corporate adjustment later recorded as EJ-CTR-09. The panel explicitly considered that the absence of data should not lead to a zero estimate, and that conservative, expert-based figures are preferable while methodologies mature.

documents.title: Implementation and pre-production test report – CTR climate module

sections.heading: Scope and test approach
sections.text: This report documents the implementation testing of the CTR climate module (MDL-19, version 1.0) in the Bank's stress testing platform (STP), performed between 12 April and 4 June 2027 in the STP pre-production environment. The tests cover the implementation specification CTR-IS v1.0 (approved by the Model Owner on 2 April 2027), the record-level reconciliation of production and development outputs, the comparison of development and production data lineage, a parallel run against the interim approach, the reconciliation with downstream systems and user acceptance testing. The module will be used in production only after the approval for use (G3) and the go-live gate (G4); until then it is deployed in pre-production only. Report version 1.0 was approved by the Model Owner and the Head of Enterprise Stress Testing on 10 June 2027.

sections.text: Implementation testing was performed by the STP test team of Enterprise Stress Testing IT, which is independent of the authors of the production code (the STP development team) and of the CTR development team in Sustainability Risk Modelling. Test cases and expected outputs were provided by the CTR developers from the development code, but test execution, defect logging and retesting were performed by the independent testers. The test lead signed the test report on 4 June 2027.

sections.heading: Test cases, defects and retesting
sections.text: All 186 specified test cases were executed, covering input data mapping and transformations, missing, invalid and boundary values (label A++++ and G, carbon price 0 and EUR 800, zero revenue), and outputs for every label class, sector and country. 183 test cases passed in the first run; three defects were logged in ticket system project CTR: CTR-311 (rounding of the energy-cost-to-income ratio to two decimals instead of four), CTR-314 (NACE 35.11 mapped to the gas supply sector instead of power generation) and CTR-318 (sector multiplier cap not applied to obligors with a missing country code). All three defects affected model outputs; they were resolved, retested and closed before 28 May 2027, and the full regression set was re-executed without failures. The test plan, test cases, results and defects are documented in the test repository (test plan TP-CTR-1.0).

sections.text: A parallel run of CTR and the interim expert-based climate add-on was performed on the reference dates 31 December 2026 and 31 March 2027, covering the full STP production cycle for the ICAAP climate adverse scenario. Operational issues were limited to the run time of the corporate module (initially 5.1 hours, reduced to 2.2 hours by parallelisation). The parallel run covers more than the one reference date required for a Tier 2 model.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD §1.2 records materiality High (exposure criterion (a), portfolios above EUR 10 billion) and complexity High, which yields Tier 1 under the §6.4 matrix; the provisional Tier 2 is justified only by the Pillar 2 nature of the output, which is not a criterion of MRM-STD-010, and a tier below the matrix outcome is not permitted.

mitigation.text: Re-submit the tiering template to MRM before G1; if Tier 1 is confirmed, plan MRC approval, annual validation, quarterly monitoring and Tier 1 implementation requirements (parallel run over three monthly reference dates).

deficiencies.rationale: Physical and transition risk are modelled separately and added at aggregation level (MDD §8, limitation L-09); the adverse scenario does not capture compound effects or amplification beyond simple aggregation.

mitigation.text: Develop a compound scenario (for example flood event combined with disorderly transition for label E–G collateral in flood-prone areas) for version 2.0; until then report a qualitative compound-risk assessment with the ICAAP results.

deficiencies.rationale: For the pass-through rates the panel minutes record individual contributions and the aggregation, but the stranded-asset haircuts (EJ-CTR-07) were set by plenary consensus without recording individual estimates (EJP §5).

mitigation.text: Repeat the elicitation of the stranded-asset haircuts with individual written estimates and rationales and update the EJ log entry EJ-CTR-07.

deficiencies.rationale: The materiality input and the scenario analysis cover climate transition risk only; ecosystem degradation and biodiversity loss are not assessed quantitatively, and physical drivers are outside the model.

mitigation.text: Record the scope limitation in the limitations log and in the materiality assessment; include a nature-related sector heatmap (agriculture, food processing) in the 2027 materiality assessment.

deficiencies.rationale: The +5% adjustment for estimated energy labels (MDD §6) is derived from a deterministic one-class shift; an independent sensitivity using the EL-EST v2 hold-out confusion matrix (probabilistic label assignment) increases mortgage losses by 11.3%, so the uncertainty from proxied labels is not adequately reflected.

mitigation.text: Recalibrate EJ-CTR-06 on a probabilistic label assignment using the EL-EST confusion matrix (at least +12% on mortgage module results) and update the limitations log and results.

validationTests.detail: RDS rebuilt from source snapshots with tag rds-v1.0.0: 612,400 loans, 3,850 obligors, 2,380 panel default events and 540 corporate default events reproduced exactly; key-variable distributions identical.

Code-versus-documentation check: label G haircut 0.100 in collateral.py L142 against 0.125 in MDD §4.2; mortgage losses under CTR-ST-ADV understated by EUR 9.6 million (7.3% of the mortgage increment).

Independent sensitivity with probabilistic label assignment (EL-EST confusion matrix) increases mortgage losses by 11.3% against the 5% conservative adjustment; carbon price and pass-through sensitivities reproduced within 2%.

MV challenger (top-down NGFS gross value added with MV sector elasticities) gives corporate losses of EUR 246 million against EUR 287 million; divergence explained by obligor-level emission intensities.
Default rates per label group in the affordability panel versus the 2025–2026 portfolio: no significant difference at 5% (two-sample test p-values 0.12–0.31).
